extracted.intended_audience: academic authors (particularly book authors submitting to university/academic presses), scholars in the humanities and social sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and philosophical advice for authors receiving harsh or critical peer review reports on academic book manuscripts, including emotional management, diagnosing reviewer comments, revising strategy, and communicating with editors. Focus is on using reviews to improve the book while protecting professional relationships and project vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go ahead and vent—but be careful about where and how you do so.
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s natural to express frustration, but avoid too much detail in semi-public forums and don’t linger in venting; the reviewer may be within your wider network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It’s fine to get support online or from peers, but avoid publicly naming or overly detailing the reviewer’s comments. After initial venting, share the report with a trusted friend or colleague for a second perspective. If helpful, write a scathing response to get the feelings out, but file that draft away rather than sending it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share the report with a trusted colleague for feedback.
rubrics_metrics.description: Get another reader’s perspective to identify productive advice you may have missed or misread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A colleague may see value you didn’t and can help you reframe comments. Use their input to decide which reviewer suggestions are substantive and which stem from misreading or different expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on problems, not solutions.
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to what issue the reviewer is pointing to (the problem) rather than fixating on their particular proposed fix (the solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reviewer suggests adding a chapter or discussing a tangential critic, ask why the reviewer is tripping up: is the point buried, unclear, or insufficiently emphasized? Often two readers will point to the same problem even if they propose different solutions. Your task is to identify and address the underlying problem so you can devise an appropriate revision plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose why the reader is tripping up (clarify and highlight buried points).
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a reviewer’s misunderstanding reflects a problem in the manuscript’s presentation (e.g., a claim is buried or not articulated strongly enough) rather than simply the reviewer’s error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the point exists in the manuscript but was missed, revise to make it clearer—move or highlight claims, strengthen articulation, or reorganize so readers will grasp your argument. Treat repeated notes from multiple reviewers as signals about where clarity is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify your vision.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reviewer comments to sharpen what you want the book to accomplish and to ensure all parts support that mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: are you trying to shift a scholarly conversation, revise an accepted history, offer a theoretical tool? Clarifying the book's goals helps you decide which advice to accept and which to decline. Remember pressures (tenure, departmental expectations) but prioritize your own ambitions and the audiences you want to reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to your editor.
rubrics_metrics.description: After processing the reports, consult (by email or meeting) with your editor to gain their perspective on audience fit and why a reviewer may have been frustrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors know the intended readership and can advise whether reviewer criticism reflects a mismatch in audience expectations or a fixable clarity problem. In some cases a negative review leads to rejection; in others an editor will partner with you on revisions. Communicate preliminary thoughts and questions to the editor and be open to their guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remember that the review process is part of a larger scholarly conversation.
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat reviews like conference feedback: mostly intended to be helpful and a chance to learn and respond, even when delivered harshly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While mean-spirited reviewers exist, most readers invest time to engage with your work. Receive comments in the spirit of scholarly exchange, be grateful someone engaged seriously with your manuscript, and take what you can from the conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your response about you, not the reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a response to reader reports, focus on what you will do to improve the book rather than enumerating how the reviewer was wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide solutions: offer a clear, concise overview of the book's intervention if argumentation was unclear; explain structural adaptations or steps to make the structure more visible; lay out a concrete revision plan. If you disagree with a reviewer, explain why and how you will realize your vision, but avoid personal attacks—keep any scathing drafts private.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold your ground when necessary and explain choices.
rubrics_metrics.description: You should defend substantive choices you truly believe in, but do so by explaining your rationale and how you will make the project succeed on your terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you really disagree with a reviewer’s take, state your position clearly in the response and describe how your planned revisions will make your vision come to life. Being willing to tackle tough criticism productively is seen positively by editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to cut your losses.
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when a negative review cannot be productively addressed for this project or press, and be prepared to move on to a different press or revise your strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes rejection or an intractable review response means it’s best to set the report aside and pursue other venues. Use the strategies above to try to salvage the project, but accept that moving on may be the appropriate decision.
